title: THE PROPHETS DIDN’T ONLY CONDEMN SEXUAL SIN—THEY EXPOSED SEXUAL HYPOCRISY
paragraphs: THE PROPHETS DIDN’T ONLY CONDEMN SEXUAL SIN—THEY EXPOSED SEXUAL HYPOCRISY
We learned how to condemn the sins happening in somebody else’s bedroom. The prophets asked what was hiding in our own hearts—and Jesus brought the question all the way to the cross.
There is a terrifying kind of Christianity that knows exactly what everybody else is doing wrong.
It can identify sexual immorality in seconds.
It can quote the verses.
It can condemn adultery.
It can rage against pornography.
It can warn about fornication.
It can speak about homosexuality.
It can defend biblical marriage.
And some of those warnings are necessary.
Sexual sin is real.
God does care what we do with our bodies.
Jesus did not come to redefine holiness until sin became meaningless.
But there is another question we rarely ask.
What if you can be right about somebody else’s sexual sin...
and still be hiding from God yourself?
What if the scandal Heaven is confronting is not merely the sin you can see in another person—but the hypocrisy you have learned to excuse in yourself?
That question is uncomfortable.
The prophets intended it to be.
Because when you actually read them, something becomes impossible to ignore.
They condemned sexual immorality, yes.
But they refused to let religious people use someone else’s sexual sin as camouflage for their own greed, cruelty, dishonesty, exploitation, pride, idolatry, injustice, and secret rebellion.
Amos is devastating.
Israel had become religious enough to maintain worship while becoming corrupt enough to crush vulnerable people.
And in Amos 2:7, economic oppression and sexual sin appear in the same prophetic indictment: the poor are trampled, justice is denied, and sexual corruption profanes the holy name of God.
Listen to the Hebrew behind that final accusation.
The text speaks of profaning God’s holy name—לְמַעַן חַלֵּל שֵׁם קָדְשִׁי, lema'an ḥallel shem qodshi—“so as to profane My holy name.”
The scandal was not merely that people had sinned sexually.
They carried the name of God while living in ways that desecrated the God whose name they carried.
That changes the question.
Because suddenly we are not talking only about them.
We are talking about us.
The worship leader with pornography hidden behind a password.
The married Christian maintaining conversations that would devastate a spouse if discovered.
The preacher condemning lust while feeding his own.
The believer posting Bible verses while humiliating people in private.
The church member who can explain biblical sexuality but cannot control bitterness.
The person furious about cultural immorality while cheating employees, neglecting the poor, lying in business, destroying people through gossip, or refusing to forgive.
Different sins.
Same terrifying possibility.
A holy vocabulary wrapped around an unrepentant heart.
Jeremiah walked straight into that contradiction.
The people trusted the temple.
They possessed religious identity.
They had sacred language.

And yet Jeremiah confronted them with an almost breathless accusation: stealing, murder, adultery, falsehood, idolatry—and then appearing before God as though religious proximity could make rebellion safe. Read Jeremiah 7 carefully. The prophet does not isolate adultery as though everything else suddenly becomes irrelevant. He exposes an entire architecture of hypocrisy.
In other words...
You cannot use church attendance to baptize secret sin.
You cannot sing louder than your disobedience.
You cannot post enough Scripture to make hidden rebellion holy.
You cannot point at another sinner long enough to make God stop looking at your heart.
And perhaps nowhere is our selective reading exposed more powerfully than in Ezekiel’s description of Sodom.
Yes, Genesis presents Sodom as profoundly sexually corrupt and violently depraved. Scripture never requires us to pretend otherwise.
But Ezekiel refuses to let us reduce Sodom’s wickedness to the one category we find easiest to weaponize against somebody else.
“Behold, this was the guilt of your sister Sodom...”
Then comes the indictment:
pride...
abundance of food...
prosperous ease...
and failure to strengthen the poor and needy.
The Hebrew imagery is striking. Ezekiel speaks of גָּאוֹן, ga'on—pride, exaltation, arrogance—and שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם, siv'at-leḥem—fullness or abundance of bread.
They had plenty.
Someone else had nothing.
And they did not “strengthen the hand” of the poor and needy.
Ezekiel is not denying Sodom’s sexual wickedness. The following verse continues the indictment by describing their arrogance and abominations.
He is making the indictment bigger.
Sodom was not merely sexually disordered.
Sodom was proud.
Self-satisfied.
Abundant.
Comfortable.
And indifferent to suffering.
That should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to condemn Sodom...
while living comfortably inside part of Sodom’s indictment.
It is possible to rage against sexual immorality while worshiping money.
To defend marriage while neglecting your spouse.
To condemn adultery while consuming pornography.
To preach purity while exploiting vulnerable people.
To defend unborn children while despising struggling mothers.
To talk about family values while refusing to forgive your own family.
To call the culture wicked while secretly enjoying the very darkness you publicly condemn.
That is sexual hypocrisy.
And the prophets hated it because God hates masks.
Not imperfect people.
Masks.
There is a difference.
God has always had room for broken people who come into the light.
David committed devastating sexual sin and arranged a man's death. Nathan confronted him. David could no longer hide behind kingship, power, reputation, or religious language.
And when David finally broke, he did not say, “But look at what everybody else is doing.”
He said, in substance, I have sinned against the LORD.
That is repentance.
Repentance stops managing appearances.
Repentance stops comparing.
Repentance stops saying, “At least I’m not like them.”
Repentance walks into the light without negotiating.
Maybe that is why this hurts.
Because some of us became experts at noticing the speck while quietly protecting the plank.
We know which politicians are immoral.
Which celebrities are immoral.
Which movements are immoral.
Which lifestyles are immoral.
Which generation is immoral.
Which denomination is compromised.
Which neighbor is living in sin.
But tonight, when the room becomes quiet and nobody is watching...
what does Jesus see?
Not your ministry title.
Not your church attendance.
Not the Bible verse in your bio.
You.
The unedited you.
The search history.
The fantasy.
The resentment.
The messages.
The pride.
The secret relationship.
The money nobody knows about.
The person you refuse to forgive.
The private compromise you renamed “struggle” years ago because “repentance” would require you to change.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come because clean people needed congratulations.
He came because sinners needed resurrection.
The answer to hypocrisy is not pretending harder.
It is coming into the light.
The answer to sexual sin is not merely public shame.
It is repentance, forgiveness, cleansing, and a transformed life in Christ.
The answer to pride is not finding a worse sinner.
It is falling before a better Savior.
Jesus does something astonishing with sinners.
He refuses both cheap condemnation and cheap grace.
He does not say sin does not matter.
And He does not say your sin means mercy is impossible.
Grace tells the truth about both.
Your sin is worse than your excuses admit.
Christ's mercy is greater than your shame can imagine.
That is the cross.
At Calvary, God did not shrug at evil.
He judged sin.
And the judgment our rebellion deserved fell upon the sinless Son who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus was not crucified because sin was insignificant.
He was crucified because sin was deadly.
And He rose because death would not have the final word.
That means the sexually broken can be redeemed.
The adulterer can repent.
The porn addict can come into the light.
The sexually abused can know that another person's evil did not make them dirty before God.
The hypocrite can remove the mask.
The proud can bow.
The greedy can become generous.
The bitter can forgive.
The religious performer can finally stop performing.
The prodigal can come home.
And the person who has spent years condemning everybody else can finally whisper the prayer Heaven has been waiting to hear:
“Jesus... deal with me.”
Maybe that is the prayer this generation desperately needs.
Not merely:
“Lord, fix them.”
But:
“Lord, search me.”
Expose what I excuse.
Break what I protect.
Reveal what I hide.
Forgive what I confess.
Heal what sin has wounded.
Teach me holiness without arrogance.
Teach me truth without cruelty.
Teach me conviction without hypocrisy.
Teach me grace without compromise.
Make my private life agree with my public faith.
Because biblical holiness is not selective outrage.
It is surrender.
And biblical grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the astonishing mercy of God that receives sinners and begins transforming them into the likeness of Christ.
Sit with that discomfort.
Maybe conviction is not God pushing you away.
Maybe it is mercy refusing to leave you hidden.
Be honest.
What did this expose?
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Do not name another person's sin.
Do not expose somebody else's scandal.
Talk about what Jesus is doing in you.
Not because sharing an article earns favor with God. It does not.
Someone may be preaching while drowning.
Someone may be smiling while ashamed.
Someone may believe that because Christians have condemned their sin, Jesus must have rejected them too.
Let them discover the truth.
Christ does not call sinners to hide.
He calls sinners to come.
Scripture gives us a beautiful guardrail here.
In Malachi 3:8 the Hebrew distinguishes the ma'aser—מַעֲשֵׂר, the tithe or tenth—from the terumah—תְּרוּמָה, a contribution or offering. Under the New Testament, Paul tells believers:
“ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης”
hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia... mē... ex anankēs
Each should give as he has determined in his heart—not under compulsion.
Then comes the beautiful phrase:
“ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.”
Hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos.
God loves a cheerful giver. — 2 Corinthians 9:7
It does not.
We cannot make that claim from Scripture.
It helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep putting the Gospel in front of people who might never walk through a church door.
And sometimes glorifying God with our resources really does look wonderfully ordinary: supporting faithful Gospel work so that more people can hear about Jesus.
It is mission.
It is helping truth travel farther.
It is helping another exhausted believer encounter Scripture at midnight.
It is helping another prodigal hear that home is still open.
It is helping another ashamed sinner discover that repentance is not the end of their story.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help enormously.
Send it privately to somebody who needs it.
Pray for this ministry.
Pray for the people reading.
Pray that we never become more interested in reach than repentance, more interested in numbers than souls, or more interested in defending Christianity than actually becoming like Christ.
Because eventually every mask falls.
Every hidden room opens.
Every excuse runs out.
And when that moment comes, our hope will never be that we managed to look cleaner than somebody else.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus.
The Friend of sinners who never became a friend of sin.
The Savior who tells the truth without abandoning the guilty.
The Lamb who carried our shame.
The King who conquered the grave.
The Christ who can take the chapter you are most ashamed of and refuse to let it become the final chapter.
Maybe your scandal is sexual.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe greed.
Maybe hypocrisy.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe something nobody knows.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His mercy.
Then get up and follow Jesus.
Because the most shocking thing about your story does not have to be what you did in darkness.
It can become what Jesus did after you finally stepped into His light.
Your scandal may explain the chapter—but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
